summary: This standards-track document defines a metadata format an OAuth 2.0 client can use to learn how to talk to an authorization server, including its endpoint locations and capabilities.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a web app can ask a user to log in through an OAuth server, it has to know where that server's pages and endpoints are. This RFC says where to look for that information: a small JSON file published at a predictable address.

questions: what is oauth authorization server metadata
how does an oauth client discover endpoints
what is the oauth issuer identifier
how does oauth metadata prevent mix-up attacks
subtitle: A standard way for a client to discover how to talk to an authorization server.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 client that has only an issuer identifier does not know where the authorization and token endpoints are, or which grant types and authentication methods the server supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a JSON metadata document, published at a well-known location derived from the issuer identifier, that lists the endpoints and the capabilities of the authorization server.
tldr.outcome: A client can fetch one document and learn everything it needs to start an authorization request, and the issuer value in that document must match the identifier it asked for, which stops an attacker from passing off a server of their own as the real one.

today: RFC 8414 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for OAuth 2.0 authorization server metadata.

sections.title: What Authorization Server Metadata Is For
sections.content:
This specification generalizes the metadata format defined by OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 in a way that stays compatible with it while applying to a wider set of OAuth 2.0 use cases. It is deliberately parallel to the way that the OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol generalized the dynamic client registration mechanisms of OpenID Connect Dynamic Registration 1.0, again compatibly.

The metadata for an authorization server is retrieved from a well-known location as a JSON document, and it declares the endpoint locations and the capabilities of the authorization server.

The metadata can be communicated in two ways. The server can assert it itself over HTTPS, or it can be a set of signed metadata values carried as claims in a JSON Web Token (JWT). In the JWT case the issuer is vouching for the validity of the data about the authorization server, which is analogous to the role the Software Statement plays in OAuth dynamic client registration.

How the client chooses an authorization server is out of scope. In some cases its issuer identifier is configured by hand into the client; in others it is discovered dynamically, for instance with WebFinger.
sections.plainLanguage: The client is usually given only the name of the server. The metadata document fills in the rest: the addresses of the endpoints and what the server can do.

sections.title: The Metadata Members
sections.content:
The issuer member is required. It is the issuer identifier, a URL that uses the https scheme and has no query or fragment components. It is used to prevent authorization server mix-up attacks.

The authorization_endpoint member gives the URL of the authorization endpoint and is required unless no supported grant type uses that endpoint. The token_endpoint member gives the URL of the token endpoint and is required unless only the implicit grant type is supported. The jwks_uri member is optional and gives the URL of the JSON Web Key Set document holding the signing keys the client uses to validate signatures from the server; it must use the https scheme, and it may also hold the server's encryption keys, in which case a use parameter is required for every key in the set.

Several members describe what the server can do. scopes_supported is recommended and lists the scope values the server supports, though a server may leave some out. response_types_supported is required and lists the response type values. response_modes_supported is optional and defaults to query and fragment. grant_types_supported is optional and defaults to authorization_code and implicit. token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported is optional and defaults to client_secret_basic, the HTTP Basic Authentication scheme of OAuth 2.0, and token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported lists the signing algorithms allowed for the private_key_jwt and client_secret_jwt methods, and must be present if either of those methods is listed. Servers should support RS256, and the value none must not be used.

Other optional members point at further endpoints, such as registration_endpoint, revocation_endpoint and introspection_endpoint, each with its own list of supported client authentication methods, and code_challenge_methods_supported, which lists the Proof Key for Code Exchange methods the server supports and, when absent, means it does not support PKCE. Members such as service_documentation, ui_locales_supported, op_policy_uri and op_tos_uri point at human-readable information. Additional metadata parameters may also be used, some defined by other specifications such as OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Two members are the address of the server and its two main endpoints. The rest describe what the server supports, so a client can pick a grant type and a way to authenticate that will actually work.

sections.title: Where the Metadata Lives
sections.content:
An authorization server that supports metadata MUST make a JSON document with the metadata available at a path formed by inserting a well-known URI string into the issuer identifier, between the host component and the path component if there is one. The default well-known URI string is /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, the path must use the https scheme, and the suffix used must be registered in the IANA Well-Known URIs registry.

Different applications may define and register their own suffixes, for example an application with its own metadata values might register and use an example-configuration suffix. Many will use the default, which is the right choice for general-purpose authorization servers. An application using this specification MUST state which suffix it uses, and one authorization server MAY publish metadata at several well-known locations.

The metadata document MUST be queried with an HTTP GET request at that path. When the issuer identifier contains a path component, any terminating slash is removed before the well-known string is inserted between the host and the path. So for the issuer identifier https://example.com the request is GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server on host example.com, and for https://example.com/issuer1 it is GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/issuer1. Using path components allows several issuers to share one host, which some multi-tenant hosting configurations need; unlike the use of .well-known in RFC 5785, this is not about publishing general information about the host.

A successful response MUST use the 200 OK status code and return a JSON object with the application/json content type, whose members are a subset of the metadata values defined in Section 2; other claims may also be returned. Claims that return multiple values are JSON arrays, and a claim with zero elements MUST be omitted. An error response uses the applicable HTTP status code.
sections.plainLanguage: The address of the document is worked out from the server's identifier by inserting a fixed string in the middle of it. The client then fetches that address with a plain GET request.

sections.title: Signed Metadata
sections.content:
Besides plain JSON elements, the metadata may carry a signed_metadata value, which is a JSON Web Token that asserts a bundle of metadata values about the authorization server. The signed metadata MUST be digitally signed or MACed using JSON Web Signature and MUST contain an iss claim naming the party attesting to the claims. Consumers may ignore the signed metadata if they do not support the feature, and a consumer that does support it MUST give the signed values precedence over the corresponding plain JSON elements.

The signed metadata is included in the authorization server metadata JSON object as this optional member: signed_metadata, a string value consisting of the entire signed JWT. A signed_metadata value SHOULD NOT appear as a claim inside the JWT itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can also sign the whole description and publish it as one token, so a client that trusts the signature has a stronger guarantee than one that merely fetched the page.

sections.title: Compatibility with OpenID Connect Discovery
sections.content:
The identifiers /.well-known/openid-configuration, op_policy_uri and op_tos_uri contain strings referring to the OpenID Connect family of specifications, but their use here is for general OAuth 2.0 features that are not specific to OpenID Connect.

The algorithm that turns an issuer identifier into a metadata location is equivalent to the one in OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 when the issuer identifier has no path component. They differ when it does have one, because OpenID Connect Discovery appends the well-known string to the issuer identifier, giving https://example.com/issuer1/.well-known/openid-configuration, while this specification inserts it before the path component, giving https://example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration/issuer1.

Going forward, OAuth authorization server metadata locations should use the transformation defined here. In legacy environments where the OpenID Connect transformation is already used, it may be necessary during a transition period to publish metadata for issuer identifiers with a path component at both locations. During that period, applications should first try the location from this specification and only fall back to the OpenID Connect one if that retrieval fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The two discovery schemes put the fixed string in different places when the server address has a path. New deployments use the OAuth rule, and old ones can publish the same file in both places for a while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support TLS. The authorization server MUST support TLS 1.2 and MAY support additional transport mechanisms that meet its security requirements, and the client MUST perform a TLS server certificate check. Confidentiality protection MUST be applied with TLS using a ciphersuite that provides both confidentiality and integrity protection.

The client MUST perform the certificate check when making a metadata request. Checking that the server certificate is valid for the issuer identifier URL prevents man-in-the-middle and DNS-based attacks, which could otherwise trick a client into using an attacker's keys and endpoints and so let the attacker impersonate the legitimate authorization server and reach the resources the client can reach.

An attacker may also try to impersonate an authorization server by publishing a metadata document that carries the issuer identifier of the server being impersonated but with the attacker's own endpoints and signing keys. The client MUST therefore check that the issuer identifier it used as the prefix of the metadata request exactly matches the value of the issuer member in the document it received, and the metadata validation rule in Section 3.3 says the same thing: if the two values are not identical, the data in the response MUST NOT be used.

Publishing metadata in a standard format makes it easier for both legitimate clients and attackers to use the server, so the same defences apply whether the metadata is published in the standard format or in an ad hoc one. The specification assumes that the client has some way of determining the appropriate protected resources to use with an authorization server and is using the correct metadata for each one. If an inappropriate protected resource is used, an attacker may be able to act as a man-in-the-middle proxy to a valid protected resource without the authorization server or the client noticing.
sections.plainLanguage: The client has to check two things: that the secure connection really reaches the server it asked for, and that the document says the same issuer the client started from. Together those stop an attacker from substituting their own server.

sections.title: The Metadata Registry
sections.content:
The specification establishes the IANA OAuth Authorization Server Metadata registry, which records each metadata member name and a reference to the specification that defines it. Names are registered on a Specification Required basis after a two-week review period on the OAuth extensions review mailing list, on the advice of one or more Designated Experts, who may also approve a registration before publication once satisfied that the specification will be published.

Each entry has a metadata name, which is case sensitive and may not match another registered name in a case-insensitive way unless the Designated Experts state a compelling reason; a metadata description; a change controller, which is the IESG for Standards Track documents; and a reference to the specification document that defines the member.

The Designated Experts must either require that metadata names and values use only printable ASCII characters, excluding the double quote and the backslash, or, for values that use other code points, require that their definitions specify the exact sequences of code points used to represent them, and must not accept registrations whose code points can only be written as escaped characters in a JSON string.
sections.plainLanguage: New metadata names are reviewed before they are recorded, and each one has to say what it means and who is responsible for it.
